tldr: This study thoroughly evaluates whether policies trained on real robots exhibit identical behavior and success rates in simulation across 22 task pairs and detailed system identification. Achieving a task score correlation of 0.9686, the authors demonstrate that simulation evaluation can reflect real-robot performance with exceptional fidelity.
hero_caption: Real-robot environments (rows 1 and 3) alongside their 1-to-1 counterpart scenes faithfully recreated in simulation (rows 2 and 4). Across four robot configurations—G1 Omnipicker, G2 Swiftpicker, G2 Wuji, and Arx X5—diverse task environments spanning rigid object picking to clothes folding are reproduced.
overview:
In robot learning, simulation evaluation is highly attractive because it is safe and fast. However, if a policy scores high in simulation but constantly fails when deployed on a real robot, the benchmark becomes meaningless. This reality gap stems not just from arm trajectories, but from discrepancies across various physical phenomena: object geometry, contact friction, deformation, and grasp stability.

To address this, the authors built the "Genie Sim Benchmark," a comprehensive evaluation platform for embodied AI models, and proposed a "Real2Sim pipeline" to rigorously examine how closely real and simulated task evaluations align. In this setup, a foundation model ($\pi_{0.5}$) fine-tuned on real-robot data runs under identical placements and instruction conditions in both the real world and simulation, and the results are compared.

The evaluation covers 4 robot configurations and 16 task names (22 task pairs in total). It also conducts detailed system identification on the bimanual G2 robot (identifying robot inertia and friction parameters) and identifies contact parameters across 5 representative objects.

As a result, a remarkably strong Pearson correlation of 0.9686 (mean absolute error of 0.0405) was confirmed between real and simulated task scores. Furthermore, system identification reduced score errors by about 20%, revealing that aligning fidelity down to physical behavior—rather than merely checking task success—is essential for trustworthy simulation evaluation.
contributions: Demonstrating a high agreement between real and simulated evaluation scores across 4 robot configurations and 16 tasks (22 task pairs in total), reaching a correlation coefficient of 0.9686.
Extending paired real–simulation evaluations beyond rigid-body manipulation to deformable object tasks, such as folding towels and clothes.

Constructing a phased system-identification framework that sequentially estimates link inertia, armature inertia, and nonlinear friction for a bimanual robot, verifying strong position and torque tracking on real teleoperation trajectories.
Systematically analyzing how object contact behavior and friction identification results transfer across distinct physics engines, including MuJoCo, MJWarp, and PhysX.

sections.heading: How Well Does Simulation Evaluation Reflect the Real Robot?
sections.summary: The true value of a simulation benchmark depends on how faithfully its results reflect real-robot behavior and performance. This section introduces the reality gap challenge—encompassing object contact and geometry beyond mere joint tracking—and sets the scope of the study.
sections.details:
The fundamental problem facing simulation-based evaluation is that success in simulation does not guarantee success in the real world. Even with matching arm kinematics, slight deviations in initial object pose, surface friction, impact restitution, or torsional resistance can easily flip grasping or handover outcomes from success to failure.

In other words, building a truly useful simulation benchmark requires more than running isolated tasks. One must systematically and structurally investigate what range of tasks to cover and which physical parameter errors dictate success or failure.

Through the "Genie Sim Benchmark" platform, this study conducts 22 final evaluation task pairs alongside 14 paired experiments comparing pre- and post-system identification (SysID). Combining robot identification experiments (G2 crsB) with contact experiments on 5 representative objects (spanning grasping, handover, and compliant contact), the work dissects simulator fidelity from two complementary angles: task outcome scores and physical-response consistency (position, torque, and contact).

sections.heading: Full Scope of the Real-to-Sim Benchmark and Its Remarkable Correlation
sections.summary: This section details 78 task definitions across four capability dimensions—instruction following, spatial reasoning, robustness, and general manipulation—alongside the paired 1-to-1 evaluation protocol. Running models fine-tuned on real-robot data yielded an exceptionally high Pearson correlation of 0.9686 across 22 tasks.
sections.details:
### Capability Dimensions and Task Structure
The Genie Sim Benchmark is designed to diagnose the strengths and weaknesses of embodied AI models across four capability dimensions covering 78 tasks. These include "Instruction Following" (interpreting color and shape directives), "Spatial Reasoning" (interpreting spatial relations and block placements), "Robustness" (handling lighting and background variations), and "General Manipulation" (testing composite skills like door opening, pouring, and bimanual coordination). In addition to overall success, intermediate sub-step progress and failure stages are recorded.

### Robot Configurations and Real2Sim Coverage
The experiments utilize four robot configurations: "G1 Omnipicker" (Unitree G1 with a custom gripper), "G2 Swiftpicker" (the next-generation G2 with a picker), "G2 Wuji" (featuring five-finger hands), and the "Arx X5" arm. The task families span target selection, pick-and-sort, bimanual handover, block stacking, and deformable manipulation like folding towels and clothes.

### Paired Evaluation and Scoring Mechanism
The evaluation strictly aligns real-world experimental layouts with simulated environments on a 1-to-1 basis. The evaluated model is the $\pi_{0.5}$ foundation model, supervised fine-tuned (SFT) on real-robot data. The identical model runs inference in both real and simulated setups to compute average stage-completion scores. Real-world trials are judged by human evaluators, while the simulator applies automated scoring under the exact same criteria.

### Score Alignment Between Real and Sim
Across all 22 evaluation pairs, the real–simulation score difference yielded a mean absolute error (MAE) of just 0.0405, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0520, and signed differences bounded between -0.110 and +0.080. The Pearson correlation reached an impressive 0.9686. Furthermore, across the 14 pairs evaluated with system identification, MAE improved from 0.0554 to 0.0443 (a roughly 20.0% reduction). This confirms that aligning simulated physical parameters with reality clearly enhances task-level score fidelity.

sections.heading: The Real2Sim Pipeline: Behind the Scenes of Trajectory Replay and Physical Verification
sections.summary: This section explains the architecture of the Real2Sim pipeline, which feeds recorded real-world commands into simulation to faithfully reproduce robot and object dynamics. The approach avoids artificial physics shortcuts, treating objects as free rigid bodies throughout.
sections.details:
### An Execution Stack Without Physical Shortcuts
The core of the Real2Sim pipeline lies in replaying recorded real-robot commands directly in simulation and observing simulator responses. In experiments with the G2 robot, 22-DoF joint position targets and 2 gripper position commands are streamed to the simulator at approximately 100 Hz, stepping physics integration forward in 1 ms sub-steps.

Crucially, the system never "welds" or suctions objects to grippers upon contact, nor does it override object poses using inverse kinematics (IK). Objects remain free rigid bodies in the simulation space from start to finish, held and transported solely through contact and friction forces. To examine cross-engine discrepancies, the pipeline supports three backends: MuJoCo (loading MJB models), GPU-parallelized MuJoCo-Warp (MJWarp), and NVIDIA PhysX with its distinct contact semantics.

### What Is Measured and How It Is Evaluated
The pipeline strictly distinguishes between tracking fidelity against real observations, cross-engine trajectory agreement, and physical task completion. Specifically, it tracks 3D object center-of-mass RMSE (in millimeters) and RGB image-space tracking errors (in pixels). Because visual features and camera views differ by task, the authors deliberately avoid collapsing these metrics into an arbitrary single percentage, choosing instead to track raw physical quantities rigorously.

sections.heading: System Identification: From Robot Joint Torques to Object Contact Friction
sections.summary: This section details the three-stage estimation of joint friction, armature inertia, and link inertia on the bimanual G2 robot, alongside contact parameter identification for five representative objects. It highlights position and torque validation on an independent teleoperation trajectory, as well as the need for contact re-tuning (native adaptation) in PhysX.
sections.details:
### Phased System Identification on the Bimanual G2 Robot
Accurate arm simulation demands precise knowledge of motor and gearbox properties alongside rigid-body dynamics. For the G2 arms (7 DoF per arm), there are 98 unknown parameters; optimizing them all at once risks failure due to parameter correlation (multicollinearity). To solve this, the authors adopted a three-stage estimation using decoupled excitation trajectories:

- **Stage 1 (Friction Identification)**: Single joints cycle through 20 constant velocity levels, robustly isolating Coulomb friction $f_c$ and viscous friction $f_v$ after canceling gravity and offsets.
- **Stage 2 (Armature Inertia Identification)**: Sinusoidal motions from 0.5 to 1.5 Hz isolate acceleration-dependent armature inertia ($J_a$) from link inertia.
- **Stage 3 (Multi-Joint Coupled Fourier Identification)**: All 7 joints execute 5th-order Fourier trajectories simultaneously for about 100 s, optimizing link inertial parameters (mass, center of mass, inertia tensor) and torque biases while holding friction and armature terms fixed.

To validate the identified parameters, a separate 32.65 s teleoperation trajectory—completely excluded from identification—was replayed in simulation. Per-joint position tracking RMSE across both arms spanned 0.00614–0.03522 rad, and current-derived torque RMSE spanned 0.735–4.001 N·m, showing excellent fidelity.

### Contact Parameter Identification for 5 Representative Objects and PhysX Challenges
To boost manipulation fidelity, five representative objects were evaluated: a kettle and gum box representing grasping and transport, a sponge for compliant contact, and a badminton shuttlecock and pen for handover and rotational resistance.

Directly transferring contact parameters identified in MuJoCo into PhysX led to failures, such as failing to lift the sponge or the shuttlecock rolling away before being grasped. These issues stemmed from differences in solver implementations and contact models. Once fingertip contact stiffness, damping, and angular damping were re-tuned natively within PhysX, all tasks replayed successfully. This experimentally proved that blindly copying parameters across engines is insufficient; native adaptation matching each engine's contact semantics is essential.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Dual Evaluation of Outcomes and Physics Paves the Way for Simulation
sections.summary: A summary of how the Genie Sim Benchmark establishes simulation fidelity through dual evaluation: aligning task outcome scores and physical response dynamics. It lays the groundwork for using simulation as a dependable surrogate for real-robot evaluation.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated an exceptionally strong score correlation of 0.9686 between real robots and simulation across 22 diverse robot–task pairs. This provides clear evidence that simulation-based evaluation can serve as a dependable indicator of real-world performance.

The paper's greatest contribution lies in moving beyond high-level success/failure comparisons to perform multi-layered physical diagnostics, covering joint torques, tracking position errors, 3D object trajectories, and cross-engine contact discrepancies. Pinpointing the exact physical sources of real-to-sim divergence enables data-driven improvements to simulator models. Looking ahead, promising directions include using vision-language models (VLMs) for initial physical parameter estimation and expanding into more adaptive interaction methods.

sections.heading: Appendix: Task Inventory and Detailed Torque Residual Data
sections.summary: Supplementary details covering the full inventory of 16 evaluation tasks, score breakdowns across robot configurations, and joint-by-joint torque residual analyses from system identification.
sections.details:
### Task Inventory and Score Details
The 16 evaluated tasks include Grasp Target Object, Select by Color, Recognize Size, Stack Blocks, Fold Towel, Folding Clothes, Bimanual Chip Handover, and Place Block Into Drawer. Each environment was evaluated across 30 to 100 rollout episodes, running an equal number of trials in reality and simulation.

### Torque Analysis in System Identification
Torque residual analysis across joints J1–J7 on both arms of the G2 robot revealed $R^2$ scores generally spanning 0.91 to 0.99, showing that the model captures real-world torque variations with high accuracy. From high-torque base joints (J1, J2) to agile wrist joints (J5–J7), quantitative data confirms that armature inertia, viscous friction, and Coulomb friction were properly decoupled and identified.

takeaways: With proper environment matching and system identification, simulation task scores can match real-robot outcomes with an extraordinary correlation exceeding 0.96.

In robot system identification, adopting a phased approach with decoupled excitation trajectories—rather than solving friction, armature inertia, and rigid-body inertia all at once—is key to physically consistent parameter estimation.
Object and fingertip contact parameters cannot simply be copied between physics engines (e.g., MuJoCo vs. PhysX); native re-calibration adapted to each engine's contact model is essential.
Improving simulators requires evaluating both task success and physical response errors (positions, torques, and 3D object trajectories) together as a unified diagnostic pair.
limitations: Evaluations on the five representative objects rely on single-episode replay trajectories, leaving independent generalization to unseen grasp poses and diverse objects to be fully proven.
Tracking of 3D object positions relies primarily on RGB-D model-based estimation rather than a ground-truth measurement setup such as optical motion capture.
Object masses were treated as fixed values from CAD/URDF priors, without addressing online mass identification or non-uniform density distributions.
